newsitem.title: USA: Jury begins deliberations in talk show murder trial.
newsitem.headline: Jury begins deliberations in talk show murder trial.

text.p: Jurors began deliberating Friday on whether to convict Jonathan Schmitz of murdering a friend who revealed his homosexual crush on a television talk show, acquit him or find him guilty of lesser charges.
Oakland County Circuit Judge Francis O'Brien read instructions to the panel of seven men and five women and sent them into the jury room shortly after 10 a.m.

Schmitz, 26, is charged with first-degree murder in the shotgun slaying of Scott Amedure, 32, on March 9, 1995, three days after Amedure revealed he had a crush on Schmitz during a taping of a "Jenny Jones" show on same-sex secret admirers.

One of the alternate jurors dismissed Friday morning told attorneys he accepted defence arguments that Schmitz, who has admitted shooting Amedure, was mentally ill at the time of the killing and unable to form the premeditated intent required for a first-degree conviction.
"His impression was that first-degree was out of the question," defence attorney Fred Gibson told reporters.

The defence contends that Schmitz was humiliated by the show because he thought he was going to meet the "girl of his dreams" when he flew to Chicago for the taping. That show never aired on television but was played during the trial.

Jurors have the option of acquitting Schmitz or finding him guilty of first-or second-degree murder, voluntary manslaughter or one of two misdemeanor charges -- careless, reckless or negligent use of a firearm causing death or discharge of a firearm causing injury while intentionally aimed without malice.
The latter charge was added to the list of jury instructions late Thursday by prosecutors, Gibson said.

The penalty for first-degree murder is life without parole. Schmitz could be sentenced to a jail term of up to life for second-degree, or eight to 15 years for manslaughter. If convicted of one of the misdemeanors, he could be released immediately because of time already served.

Since opening arguments Oct. 14, jurors heard from more than 30 witnesses including Jenny Jones, the normally bubbly talk show host, who appeared nervous and portrayed herself as having little detailed knowledge of how her show is produced.
Regardless of the outcome of the criminal trial, Jones and her show, produced by Telepictures, a unit of Warner Bros., will face a $25 million lawsuit filed by Amedure's family.
